paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Age of Discovery, also called the Age of Exploration, ran from about 1418 to about 1620. In those years, sailors from European countries explored, colonized and conquered lands across the globe. It linked parts of the world that had been cut off from one another into a single world-system, and it laid the groundwork for globalization.

paragraphs.heading: Portugal heads south and east
paragraphs.text: Portugal's ocean voyages began with trips to the Macaronesian islands, such as the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores. From 1418, sponsored by Prince Henry the Navigator, the Portuguese explored Africa's Atlantic coast step by step. Bartolomeu Dias reached the Indian Ocean this way in 1488, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa to India, opening direct trade with Asia. The Portuguese pushed on to the Spice Islands in 1512, China a year later and Japan in 1543.

paragraphs.heading: Spain sails west
paragraphs.text: In 1492 Spain's Catholic Monarchs paid for Christopher Columbus's plan to reach the Indies by sailing west across the Atlantic. He came upon a continent Europeans had not mapped, though the Norse had explored it and briefly settled there 500 years before; it was later named America after Amerigo Vespucci. In 1513 the Spaniard Vasco Núñez de Balboa made his way over the Isthmus of Panama to the 'other sea'. In 1522 an expedition led by Ferdinand Magellan, and after his death by Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the first voyage around the world.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting the globe
paragraphs.text: Portugal quickly claimed the lands Columbus reached under the Treaty of Alcáçovas. Castile, though, persuaded the Pope, himself a Castilian, to issue four papal bulls dividing the world into two zones, each giving one kingdom sole rights to claim newly found lands. The Treaty of Tordesillas later modified this split. Spain went on to conquer Mexico and Peru, and its Manila galleons tied the Americas to Asia across the Pacific from 1565 to 1815.

paragraphs.heading: The Columbian exchange
paragraphs.text: European exploration set off the Columbian exchange between the Old World, meaning Europe, Asia and Africa, and the New World of the Americas. Plants, animals, people including slaves, diseases and culture all crossed between the two hemispheres. New diseases hit American Indians especially hard, and some of their populations fell quickly. The era also brought widespread enslavement, exploitation and conquest of Indigenous peoples.

paragraphs.heading: Trade and maps
paragraphs.text: New sea routes to the East Indies and the colonization of the Americas, first by the Portuguese and Spaniards and then by the English, French and Dutch, drove the growth of global trade. Today's connected world economy grew out of the trade networks built in this era. Maps changed too: continents that European mapmakers had drawn as vague blobs turned into the outlines we recognize today.

paragraphs.heading: Whose discovery
paragraphs.text: The word discovery itself has come under scrutiny. It traces back to disco-operio, to uncover, so whatever was revealed was already there. A legal idea called the discovery doctrine, set out by the United States Supreme Court in 1823, rests on European powers' claimed right to take land they explored. Many Indigenous peoples reject colonial claims of discovery over their lands as forced and as denying that they were there. Some writers use Age of Contact or Contact Period instead.
